newsitem.title: USA: Manufacturing jump shows U.S. economy's vigor.
newsitem.headline: Manufacturing jump shows U.S. economy's vigor.

text.p: Manufacturing businesses gained renewed vigour last month as a broad-based gauge of national activity confirmed the economy began the second half with brisk momentum, reports on Tuesday said.

In separate reports, the National Association of Purchasing Management said its index showed a rise in manufacturing activity in August while the Conference Board said its Index of Leading Indicators posted a sixth consecutive monthly rise in July.

Analysts said the latest signs of buoyant growth raised doubts that the economy was slowing rapidly enough to forestall the Federal Reserve from raising interest rates -- possibly as soon as this month -- to tamp down inflationary pressures.

The NAPM index of manufacturing activity climbed to 52.6 in August after slipping to 50.2 in July from 54.3 in June, a relatively modest gain but one showing growth. A reading over 50 indicates an expanding manufacturing sector.

Underlining the economy's firm base as the second half of 1996 began, the private Conference Board said its leading index advanced in July by 0.2 percent after a 0.5 percent rise in June. It has not turned down since last January.
The index measures a basket of economic indicators, from unemployment benefit claims to building permits. Six of its 11 components were stronger in July, while five weakened from June.

Economist Cynthia Latta of DRI/McGraw Hill Inc. in Lexington, Mass., said the economy was losing some steam after a booming 4.8 percent annual rate of expansion in the second quarter, but its strength was probably still making policymakers nervous.
"I don't think anyone expects another 4.5 percent to 5 percent third quarter but the question is whether we are slowing enough to avoid overheating," Latta said.
"I think there is more momentum and more strength out there than we thought earlier and certainly more than the Fed was assuming," Latta said.

Policymakers at the U.S. central bank held off raising short-term interest rates at their last meeting on Aug. 20 but analysts think the odds that it must soon act have risen as signs mount that a sturdy spring expansion carried on into the summer with less slowing than the Fed had expected.
"The third quarter started with a whimper, but it looks like it's going to end with a bang in terms of the economic outlook," said economist David Jones at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. in New York.
"It looks like the Fed will have to tighten at the Sept. 24 meeting, if not before," Jones added.
Next Friday's scheduled report on August unemployment is widely regarded as critical, especially if upwards of 200,000 jobs were created so that wage pressures might increase.

At a weekend session in Jackson Hole, Wyo., Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan was characteristically circumspect in remarks to central bankers and economists from around the world about the economy's prospects but he dwelt on the importance of pressing the fight against inflation to secure progress already made.

"Now, for the first time in at least a generation, the goal of price stability is within reach of all the major industrial countries as well as a substantial number of others," Greenspan said at sessions where some private economists suggested higher interest rates were warranted now to sustain non-inflationary growth.
Despite the pickup in the NAPM index in August, many individual executives said the tempo of business was little changed and there were few signs of soaring prices.
"They generally think things are going to continue to improve at a slow and steady rate," said Ralph Kauffman, chairman of NAPM's business survey committee.
"There were very few comments dealing with the experiences of increased prices," he added.

But the Conference Board cited higher commodity prices as one of its six signals of rising activity during July, together with fewer new claims for unemployment benefits and more consumer goods orders.
In addition, contracts and orders for plant and equipment increased from June, there were more applications for building permits and stronger consumer expectations for the future.

The five negative indicators included a shorter average workweek, lower stock prices and faster vendor deliveries. In addition, order backlogs were smaller than in June and the money supply was lower, the Conference Board said.
